item.base_system: Polymorphic CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy in face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structures
item.intervention: Accounting for longitudinal spin fluctuations (LSFs) as a function of temperature in first-principles calculations
item.processing: First-principles alloy theory using DFT with the LSF methodology (Dong et al.) and fluctuating medium approximation
item.test_conditions: Temperature range 50 K to 1200 K; volumes represented by Wigner-Seitz radius
item.structure_change: Finite magnetic moments thermally induced for Co, Cr, and Ni at all volumes even at 50 K; mean magnetic moments {m_I} exhibit monotonic dependency on volume and temperature
item.property_change: Magnetic moments for Co, Cr, and Ni increase with temperature; e.g., at 100 K, m_Co is 0.73 μ_B (fcc) and 0.67 μ_B (hcp); at 900 K, m_Co is 1.30 μ_B (fcc) and 1.27 μ_B (hcp)
item.attributed_mechanism: LSFs induce sizable magnetic moments for Co, Cr, and Ni, whereas Fe and Mn already have large spontaneous static magnetic moments
quotes: Accounting for the LSFs at finite temperature (contour plots in Fig. 1), finite magnetic moments have been thermally induced for Cr, Ni and Co at all volumes even at the lowest temperature considered here (50 K)
The mean magnetic moment m I in both phases exhibits a monotonic dependency on volume and temperature.
LSFs induce sizable magnetic moments for Co, Cr and Ni, whilst slightly increasing the magnetic moment of Fe and Mn in both the fcc and hcp phases.

item.base_system: CoCrFeMnNi alloy in fcc and hcp phases
item.intervention: Comparison of free energy differences (ΔF_fcc→hcp) derived from Floating Spin (FS) vs. LSF schemes
item.processing: Free energy calculations F_α(w, T) = E_int(w, {M_I}) - TS_mag({M_I}) using DFT and CPA
item.test_conditions: Volume range including Wigner-Seitz radius below/above ~2.64/2.68 Bohr; Temperature 50 to 1200 K
item.structure_change: LSFs systemically lower the absolute magnitude of ΔF_fcc→hcp and promote smooth dependencies on volume and temperature
item.property_change: Critical temperature of fcc-hcp phase transition determined to be ~430 K in LSF calculations compared to ~438 K in FS calculations
item.attributed_mechanism: The noticeable changes in the shape of contour lines in the FS calculations emerge from the distinct {μ_0^I} in the fcc and hcp phases, amplified by temperature in the calculation of magnetic entropy
quotes: With respect to the Δ F fcc→hcp derived from the FS calculations, the LSFs at finite temperature systemically lower the absolute magnitude of Δ F fcc→hcp

Referring to the experimental volumes [40] indicated by stars, the critical temperature of fcc-hcp phase transition at ambient pressure is determined to be ~430 K in the LSF calculations, compared to ~438 K in the FS calculations.
The hcp phase is energetically preferable to the fcc one at cryogenic temperatures, which results in negative stacking fault energy at these conditions.

item.intervention: Calculation of intrinsic stacking fault energy (γ_isf) accounting for LSFs and thermal lattice expansion
item.processing: Thermodynamic model by Olson and Cohen using computed ΔF_fcc→hcp and constant σ of 5 mJ m^-2
item.test_conditions: Temperature 50 K to 1000 K; volumes based on experimental thermal lattice expansion
item.structure_change: Stacking fault energy (γ_isf) increases with temperature, changing from negative to positive values
item.property_change: γ_isf predicted to increase from -17 mJ m^-2 at 50 K, reach zero at ~260 K, and rise to 31 mJ m^-2 at 1000 K
item.attributed_mechanism: The positive temperature dependence of γ_isf is ultimately dominated by the magneto-volume coupling at thermal excitations
quotes: Taking the experimentally determined lattice expansion (indicated by the stars) into account, the γ isf of PM CoCrFeMnNi is predicted from the LSF calculations to increase from −17 mJ m −2 at 50 K, reach zero at ~260 K and keep rising to 31 mJ m −2 at 1000 K
The hcp phase is energetically preferable to the fcc one at cryogenic temperatures, which results in negative stacking fault energy at these conditions.
With increasing temperature, the stacking fault energy increases, suppressing the formation of stacking faults and nano-twins.

item.intervention: Analysis of partial contributions to stacking fault energy (γ_isf) from internal energy (γ_isf_int) and magnetic entropy (γ_isf_mag)
item.processing: Decomposition of γ_isf = γ_isf_int + γ_isf_mag + 2σ in LSF and FS calculations
item.test_conditions: Temperature 300 K to 1200 K; various volumes
item.structure_change: LSFs considerably reduce the contribution from magnetic entropy but noticeably increase the internal energy part
item.property_change: γ_isf accounting for LSFs decreases in the most fcc-stable region by an upper change of ~13.5 mJ m^-2 (at 2.68 Bohr and 1200 K)
item.attributed_mechanism: LSFs considerably reduce the contribution emerging from the magnetic entropy γ_isf_mag (owing to the similar magnetic states in the fcc and hcp phases)
quotes: Looking at the partial contributions to γ isf shown in Fig. 3(b), it is evident that LSFs considerably reduce the contribution emerging from the magnetic entropy γ i s f mag
The positive temperature dependence of γ isf is ultimately dominated by the magneto-volume coupling at thermal excitations.

item.base_system: PM CoCrFeMnNi in fcc and hcp phases
item.intervention: Calculation of fcc-hcp interfacial energy (σ) using the Olson and Cohen model and supercell approach
item.processing: Comparison of σ derived from LSF and FS schemes with experimental lattice expansion
item.test_conditions: Temperature interval 300–900 K; extrapolation to 0 K
item.structure_change: LSFs slightly lower the interfacial energy σ compared to FS calculations
item.property_change: LSFs at finite temperature slightly lower σ by 0.5~0.7 mJ m^-2 in the temperature interval 300–900 K; σ predicted to be ~6.1 mJ m^-2 at 0 K in LSF vs 7.0 mJ m^-2 in FS
item.attributed_mechanism: The role of LSFs disclosed in PM CoCrFeMnNi is in good agreement with that reported in PM γ-Fe and Fe-22.5 at.% Mn
quotes: It is evident from Fig. 4 that the LSFs at finite temperature slightly lower σ by 0.5~0.7 mJ m −2 in the temperature interval 300–900 K.
Extrapolating our calculations to 0 K, the σ of PM CoCrFeMnNi is predicted to be ~6.1 and 7.0 mJ m −2 in the LSF and FS schemes, respectively
The σ of PM CoCrFeMnNi derived from the LSF and FS schemes is compared in Fig. 4 for different temperatures, where the experimentally determined lattice expansion [40] was accounted for.

item.intervention: Comparison of equilibrium magnetic moments {μ_0^I} from conventional floating spin (FS) calculations between fcc and hcp phases
item.processing: Conventional FS calculations solely dependent on volume
item.test_conditions: Various volumes; no temperature dependence in FS static moments
item.structure_change: Large spontaneous magnetic moments obtained for Fe and Mn at all volumes; Cr and Ni moments are zero at small volumes
item.property_change: Fe, Mn, and Co in the fcc phase exhibit larger magnetic moments than in the hcp phase at given volumes; max difference ~0.32, 0.64, and 0.28 μ_B
item.attributed_mechanism: A somewhat similar magneto-volume coupling is observed in the fcc and hcp phases for the same alloy component
quotes: In particular, in both phases large spontaneous magnetic moments are obtained for Fe and Mn at all considered volumes, whereas those of Cr and Ni are always zero and a finite magnetic moment arises only at large volumes for Co.
Comparing the magnitude of { μ 0 I } in the two phases, Fe, Mn, and Co in the fcc phase exhibit larger magnetic moments than in the hcp phase at the given volumes.
The maximum difference amounts to ~0.32, 0.64 and 0.28 μ B for Fe, Mn and Co at the radius of ~2.62, 2.62 and 2.68 Bohr, respectively.

item.intervention: Assessment of the impact of LSFs on the phase boundary (ΔF_fcc→hcp = 0)
item.processing: Free energy difference calculations with and without LSFs
item.test_conditions: Volume and temperature range 50 to 1200 K
item.structure_change: LSFs yield small influence on the phase boundary despite altering partial contributions to free energy
item.property_change: Critical temperature of fcc-hcp phase transition is ~430 K (LSF) vs ~438 K (FS); experimental value ~633 K
item.attributed_mechanism: The partial contributions to ΔF_fcc→hcp, i.e., the magnetic entropy and internal energy, may be considerably altered by LSFs at finite temperature
quotes: Nevertheless, LSFs yield small influence on the phase boundary (defined here as Δ F fcc→hcp = 0) of PM CoCrFeMnNi.

Referring to the experimental volumes [40] indicated by stars, the critical temperature of fcc-hcp phase transition at ambient pressure is determined to be ~430 K in the LSF calculations, compared to ~438 K in the FS calculations.
The hcp phase is thermodynamically stable against the fcc one at low temperatures and small volumes.

item.intervention: Evaluation of magnetic moments {m_I} as a function of temperature with thermal lattice expansion
item.processing: LSF calculations combined with experimental thermal lattice expansion data
item.structure_change: Mean magnetic moments {m_I} in both phases significantly increase with temperature
item.property_change: At 100 K, difference in m_I between fcc and hcp phases amounts to ~0.05, 0.03, 0.17, and 0.23 μ_B for Co, Cr, Fe, and Mn respectively
item.attributed_mechanism: The m_I of Fe and Mn shows more pronounced dependency on volume with respect to that on temperature, whereas LSFs give the prevailing contribution to the m_I of Co, Cr and Ni
quotes: It is evident that { m I } in both phases significantly increase with temperature, and at the given temperatures the magnetic states of the alloy components in the fcc phase are very close to those in the hcp phase.

At 100 K, the difference in m I between the two phases amounts to ~0.05, 0.03, 0.17 and 0.23 μ B for Co, Cr, Fe, and Mn, respectively, and this difference slightly reduces with increasing temperature.
The m I of Fe and Mn, the two elements exhibiting large spontaneous static magnetic moments μ 0 I , shows more pronounced dependency on volume with respect to that on temperature
